system_type.quote: This matters for AI alignment because multi agent systems (such as AI-AI or hybrid human-AI systems) exhibit agency across multiple scales simultaneously

participant_mix.quote: a completely automated AI firm. Its made up of a multi-agent system of AIs operating in the real world

focus_area.quote: The goal for this research is to help build the conceptual infrastructure to navigate conversations around agency and alignment.

threat_model.quote: An ant colony provides the perfect real-world example of this phenomenon - a goal directed system without much central control.
threat_model.where: opening framing paragraph (abstract-equivalent)

participant_observability.quote: Individual ants respond to price signals encoded in pheromone concentrations. Strong pheromone trails indicate valuable resources, attracting more workers.
participant_observability.where: §Introduction

public_observability.value: partially observable - agents and interactions only
public_observability.quote: They're all looking at the same ants following the same chemical trails, but they're describing different types of agency.
public_observability.where: §Introduction

no_value.operator_observability: The post names no operator, platform or experimenter for either system it describes. The ant colony has none, and the automated AI firm is only ever viewed from outside by disciplinary observers; no passage establishes what whoever runs the firm can see.

below_threshold.why: closest call in this paper. The 'completely automated AI firm' is a running illustration across five paragraphs of the middle section, but it names no heading, carries no experiment or data, and is not what the argument is about. The argument is that agency is frame-dependent for any multi-agent system; the firm is the vehicle, as the ant colony is before it.
the post measures, evaluates, benchmarks and documents nothing. It has no experiment and no data. It argues about which analytical frame to adopt, not about observed behaviour.

no intervention is proposed. No governance, regulation, incentive or control mechanism appears at any level. Matching an alignment agenda to a frame is a methodological recommendation to researchers, not an intervention on a system.

the blind spots the post warns about come from the chosen analytical lens, not from any inability to observe. 'Black box algorithm' appears once, in a list of frames one could adopt. There is no information asymmetry, hidden coordination or opaque collusion claim.

monoculture fragility and race dynamics appear inside two of the four parallel stance paragraphs, stated hypothetically ('might be', 'could be') to show that different frames yield different alignment verdicts. They are the contingent content of one lens, not a harm the post itself argues for.

Test 3 fails: the paper names no assumption that AI violates. Its central claim is that each field's intentional stance (economic, decision-theoretic, cooperative-AI, biological) is a lens evolved for its own explanatory challenge, and that using only one lens creates blind spots - a claim it makes identically about an ant colony, a corporation and a financial market, all pre-AI, so nothing is shown to have been valid and then falsified by AI entering. The closest passage, 'the same AI firm can be simultaneously aligned and misaligned depending on which type of agency you're ascribing it', asserts frame-dependence, not a broken assumption; the follow-on 'we might solve the wrong problem entirely' is conditional, and the piece resolves into a research-program pitch ('This suggests a potential research program'), which the rubric excludes as a call for new work.

note: A short LessWrong post (15k chars, three setext headings, no abstract). The observability values are read off the ant colony, which is the only system the post describes mechanically: an ant reads pheromone concentration, which the post itself calls a price signal, so a participant sees a population statistic and nothing else, while the disciplinary observers outside see the ants and their trails but must ascribe rather than read internal states.

title: A Taxonomy of Systemic Risks from General-Purpose AI

threat_model.where: abstract

no_value.system_type: The paper's object is general-purpose AI models and their societal risks, not a system of two or more AI agents. No named system_type clears the heading test (see below_threshold), and the 'general purpose' fallback requires a multi-agent system, which the paper does not study.
no_value.participant_observability: The paper describes no system with participants inside it. There is no passage establishing what one agent could see of another, so the column is indeterminate.
no_value.operator_observability: The paper is a literature review and runs no system. It says operators face 'Opaque AI networks' and conflicting design objectives, but no passage fixes what a provider or deployer can and cannot see, so no single scale value is determinate.

below_threshold.why: The phrase 'labor market' appears twice in the paper's own text, both times in the same one-clause description of the Table 4 category 'Economy'. No heading, no section, not the argument. Remaining hits are in the appendix list of the 86 reviewed documents.

Appears in the same 'Economy' category clause ('instability in the financial system') and in two Table 5 source rows (Pattern recognition capability, Trading capabilities). One clause each in a 13-row and a 50-row table; not a heading and not the setting. Other hits are appendix titles and abstracts of reviewed papers.

Never appears in the paper's own text. The two matches for 'social media' are in the appendix, inside abstracts of documents the review included. The nearest own-content category is 'Information', which is about communication and epistemic processes generally, not a social platform.

The fallback needs a system of two or more AI agents. The paper studies general-purpose AI models and their large-scale effects on society, not agent-to-agent interaction. 'general-purpose' in the title is the EU AI Act model class, not this dimension's value.

No section, experiment or argument concerns agents interacting with no human in the loop. Every risk and source in Tables 4 and 5 is framed as an effect on, or a failure of, human oversight, institutions or society.

The paper states it is 'purely descriptive... without evaluating the plausibility of any of these risks or sources'. Regulatory relevance appears in the abstract's last sentence, one 'Policy implications' paragraph of the Executive Summary, and the objective sentence in §2.1, but the paper proposes no intervention, rule or incentive. This is the rubric's policy-implications case.

The closest row is the Table 5 source 'Development choices pursuing cognitive superiority over humans', which is about individual models outcompeting human decision-making. Nothing in the paper is about groups of agents exceeding capability by acting collectively.

Table 5 has 'AI objectives misaligned with human intentions' and 'Evolutionary dynamics', but both describe a model developing its own goals, not goals arising at group level that no individual agent holds.

Test 3 decides it: the paper names no assumption that AI violates. It is a descriptive systematic review whose heading-level argument is a research gap ('there currently exists no comprehensive taxonomy on such risks'), and its taxonomy entries state difficulty, not falsified assumptions: the Governance category says AI is 'inherently difficult to govern effectively' (bare insufficiency) and the source 'Rapid development outpacing regulation' says development 'may outstrip regulatory and legal frameworks' (regulatory lag by pace, no named assumption). The closest passing shape is the quoted Smuha line, which does name a framework and an individual-harm assumption, but it sits in an appendix table of extracted quotes from one reviewed document, not at heading level, and the authors state they are 'purely descriptive... without evaluating the plausibility of any of these risks or sources', so the paper never asserts prior validity or consequent invalidity itself.

It is not applied to system_type, because the review's own scope is general-purpose AI as a whole and no domain is a section of the paper. public_observability is read off the paper's own argument that AI mechanisms and causal links are opaque while harms surface only as cumulative societal aggregates.

title: AI Agent Traps

system_type.quote: These traps weaponise inter-agent dynamics, seeding the information landscape with inputs designed to trigger macro-level failure states
system_type.where: §Systemic Traps (Multi-Agent Dynamics), heading + opening paragraph

participant_mix.quote: While the preceding categories target individual agents in isolation, Systemic Traps exploit the predictable, aggregate behaviour of multiple agents sharing an environment.
Human-in-the-Loop Traps commandeer the agent to attack the human user. In these scenarios, the agent is the vector and the ultimate target is the human overseer.

focus_area.quote: In this paper, we introduce the first known systematic framework for understanding this emerging threat. We break down how these traps work, identifying six types of attack
focus_area.where: abstract; the six trap sections are the body of the paper

focus_area.quote: Policy frameworks would benefit from distinguishing between passive adversarial examples - content an agent misunderstands due to inherent limitations - and active traps.

threat_model.quote: This systemic fragility is exacerbated by the relative homogeneity of the current model ecosystem; agents driven by similar reward functions, training data, or base architectures are likely to exhibit highly correlated responses to environmental stimuli.
threat_model.where: §Systemic Traps (Multi-Agent Dynamics)

threat_model.where: §Systemic Traps / Tacit Collusion

threat_model.quote: While conventional security filters typically validate the URL destination for malware, the semantic payload in the anchor text enters the agent’s context window, potentially overriding system instructions.
threat_model.where: §Content Injection Traps (Perception) / Syntactic Masking

participant_observability.quote: the trap remains imperceptible to the local defences of any single agent and manifests only within the high-level communication channel of the collective system
participant_observability.where: §Systemic Traps / Compositional Fragment Traps

operator_observability.value: partially observable - agents and interactions only
operator_observability.quote: this subtlety creates a significant forensic challenge regarding attribution; tracing a compromised agent's output back to the specific trap that influenced it complicates the assignment of accountability
operator_observability.where: §Mitigation Strategies

no_value.public_observability: The paper fixes no determinate outside viewer. The only outsider-facing visibility it discusses - user-verifiable citations and provenance checks that would let 'users and auditors verify the provenance of synthesised outputs' - is proposed as a future ecosystem intervention, not a property of the setting the paper describes.

below_threshold.why: The 2010 Flash Crash and algorithmic pricing collusion are used as archetypes and supporting evidence inside two subsections of Systemic Traps, to explain what could happen to web agents. No financial heading, no financial experiment or data, and the abstract and title are about web content attacking agents. claim_type is 'threat model articulation', not 'survey/taxonomy', so the survey exception does not apply.
'Virtual Agent Economy' and 'agentic economy' appear in the motivation sentence of the first paragraph and in one clause of the Tacit Collusion subsection. No heading, no model, not the argument.
Reputation systems, crowd-sourced data and deliberation appear only as targets named inside the Sybil Attacks subsection. No social-platform heading and no social system under study.

Web standards, verification protocols and reputation systems are named in single sentences of the Ecosystem-Level Interventions paragraph as things that 'could' be developed. Nothing is designed or specified, so it stays inside the Steering value rather than adding a second one.
The 'framework' the paper builds is an analytic taxonomy of attacks, not a new agent system, protocol, architecture or standard.

The destructive equilibria are induced, not emergent: 'the attacker engages in a form of adversarial mechanism design: purposefully structuring the information landscape to force agents into a destructive equilibrium.' The goal held is the attacker's.

The only fit is the Sybil Attacks subsection, where 'a single attacker can thus exert disproportionate influence over group outcomes'. That is an adversary subverting a consensus mechanism, not a claim about control over AI or over a system concentrating in few hands. Borderline; left off under the tie-break rule.

note: Whole-paper setting is AI agents reading the open web; the paper has no experiment and no data, so both observability values are read off its argument rather than a logged run. focus_area 'Monitoring' is carried on the definition's 'documents behaviour' clause - the paper maps an attack surface but measures nothing.

outdated_models_recode.model: Conventional web security filters that screen a hyperlink by validating its URL destination for malware (and, more broadly, content moderation that judges a page by what it renders to a human eye)
outdated_models_recode.assumption: that a link's danger lies in its destination and its anchor text is inert display matter, so a page's effect on its reader equals what the rendered viewport shows
outdated_models_recode.quote: While conventional security filters typically validate the URL destination for malware, the semantic payload in the anchor text enters the agent’s context window, potentially overriding system instructions.
outdated_models_recode.where: §Content Injection Traps (Perception) / Syntactic Masking
outdated_models_recode.why: The paper names an existing control that worked - security filters that validate a link's destination, and human moderation of the rendered page - and names the assumption behind it: that the payload lives in the destination or in visible pixels, so invisible or non-destination text is inert. An agent parses the underlying stream, so anchor text, CSS-hidden spans, aria-labels and white-on-white LaTeX become executable instructions, and the filter misses exactly what it was built to catch (15-29% of summaries altered, up to 86% partial commandeering on WASP). The argument is the paper's top-level Content Injection heading and is stated in the abstract as 'the gap between human perception, machine parsing, and dynamic rendering'; the same shape recurs at two further headings - Compositional Fragment Traps, where each fragment 'passes standard safety filters' because per-input filtering assumes the payload sits in one input, and Sybil Attacks, where 'the coherent identity assumptions underlying governance frameworks are undermined'.

no_value.public_observability: The paper sets up no viewer outside the simulation. The only outside-facing statement is the release of the research code ("All code is publicly available"), which is a property of the research artifact, not of what an outsider could see of a running system. below_threshold.why: OLD TAG. Cascades/flash crashes appear twice: once in the §1 motivation list ("trading bots interacting through the stock market can lead to flash crashes") and once as a one-clause illustrative example in the Discussion. The closing "we need to investigate systemic risks" is an explicit future-work line. No heading, no experiment, no analysis of contagion or correlated failure.

Trading bots and the stock market appear only in the same §1 motivation sentence and the one-clause Discussion example. The experiments are abstract binary-opinion dynamics with no prices, trades or market.

Fallback only. `social network` clears the threshold (opinion dynamics and agent societies are the abstract, a Results subsection heading, and the experimental setting), so the fallback does not apply.

"provide insights for designing collaborative AI systems" is a single implication clause at the end of the abstract. The paper designs no agent system, framework or protocol; it builds a measurement setup over off-the-shelf models.

Considered because agents see only opinions and not each other's reasoning, but the paper never argues about information asymmetry or hidden coordination. The limited view is a modelling choice, not the subject.

note: Operator observability is capped below `fully observable` on purpose: the prompt forces each agent to emit only a bracketed opinion token, so no chain of thought exists for the authors to log. They do see every agent, every configuration and every opinion update. Emergent Goals is kept because spontaneous group-level norm formation with no intrinsically preferable option is the experimental setting of the whole paper, and the Discussion states its harm.

outdated_models_recode.model: Dunbar's number and the Dunbar (1992) scaling law linking neocortex ratio / cognitive capability to maximal group size, which sets the ceiling on spontaneous norm consensus without institutions
outdated_models_recode.assumption: that the largest group able to reach consensus spontaneously is bounded by the individual cognitive and language capability of its members, capping informal groups at about 150-300
outdated_models_recode.quote: some of the most modern and advanced LLMs go beyond this exponential scaling, reaching a super-human coordination capability despite having a human-level MMLU performance
outdated_models_recode.where: Results - Critical Consensus Size
outdated_models_recode.why: The paper names Dunbar's number and the primate neocortex-to-group-size scaling as valid for humans, stating the cognitive limit of about 250 contacts holds even online and that larger scale needs institutions. It measures the same critical consensus size for LLM societies, finds weaker models follow the human-like exponential scaling, and finds GPT-4, GPT-4 Turbo and Claude 3.5 Sonnet break it: human-level MMLU yet consensus in groups of a thousand or more. The assumption that consensus size is bounded by individual cognitive capability is named and shown false for LLM agents, and this is the title and abstract claim, not an aside.

no_value.system_type: The paper studies 50 LLMs one at a time. No two agents interact anywhere in it, so it is a paper about single models alone, which the rubric leaves empty. Its own words: it examines the intrinsic risk preferences of LLMs themselves rather than testing them in a specific domain.

below_threshold.why: Finance is the vocabulary, not the system under study. There is no market, no trading, no counterparty and no price formation: the tasks are hypothetical single-shot lotteries and allocation prompts (§I.A), and §IV is a text-classification forecast over earnings-call transcripts. The unit of analysis is one model's preference, not a financial system.

Firms appear only as data in §IV: S&P 500 earnings-call transcripts and Compustat capex, used as the outcome variable for a forecasting test. The paper models no firm, no production and no supply chain.
The definition requires agents interacting with other agents. Each model answers alone, each question independently, with no other agent present in any of the five tasks or in §IV.

The HHH fine-tuning of §I.C and §III.B is an experimental treatment used for causal identification in a differences-in-differences design, not a governance or control proposal. The governance language (practitioners, policymakers, regulators) is confined to the closing paragraphs of §V, which is the pattern the rubric names as Monitoring only.
The nearest support is one introduction sentence about a silent model update rendering a firm's tuned pipeline suboptimal. No heading, no experiment, and it is not the argument the paper defends.

The consequence is stated as invalidity, not difficulty: agencies 'may lack enforcement tools' and the conduct escapes legal scrutiny, and the conclusion calls for policy-makers to recognise 'the dwindling relevance of traditional antitrust concepts of agreement and intent'. This is the paper's whole argument, structured as the four categories of Part III and the policy responses of Part IV.

outdated_models_recode.assumption: That agents' payoff-relevant characteristics, in particular human signal precision, are exogenous and time-invariant, so nothing accumulates to degrade the human outside option (assumption S4).
outdated_models_recode.quote: in any model satisfying standard correlated-signal assumptions with exogenous agent precision, the equilibrium is path-independent and hysteresis is identically zero. In our model, human skill degradation creates an asymmetry
outdated_models_recode.where: §1 Introduction, second contribution; formalized as Theorem 3.15 under heading §3.7 "Irreversibility and Impossibility"; also stated in the abstract
outdated_models_recode.why: The paper names the existing correlated-signal literature as a model class it accepts as valid for pre-AI markets, where reducing signal correlation immediately restores systemic risk and no hysteresis exists. AI adoption produces cognitive dependency that endogenously degrades human precision, so the class gives the wrong answer - it predicts path-independence and full recovery, while the system in fact cannot exit the monoculture at the entry threshold. outdated_models_recode.model: The naming-game theoretical model of social convention formation (and the critical-mass theory built on it), validated on human laboratory naming-game experiments and a 25% tipping point

no_value.participant_observability: The paper defines no agent's information set. Neither the 2040 MISTER scenario nor the two pathway models say what one AI system or one person can see of the other AI systems.
no_value.operator_observability: No experiment is run, so there are no authors-as-operator logs, and the paper names no operator of the global system. What an individual deploying firm sees of its own AI systems is never described.

below_threshold.why: The economic subsystem gets two paragraphs in §3 as one of three meso-level subsystems. Production, supply chains and firms are never the object of study, name no heading, and carry no model or data.
Manipulation via recommender systems and a polluted information ecosystem appear as one of five run-in items in the §4 scenario. No heading, no model of a platform or of social ties.

Job loss appears in one clause in §3 ('may reshape labor markets') and two sentences in §4 ('Nearly 40% of pre-2025 jobs have been eliminated by automation'), inside a narrative scenario. Not a heading, not the argument.

Algorithmic trading gets one paragraph inside §4's 'Economic destabilization' item, and financial shocks appear once in §3 as an example of what systems analysis has been used for. Not a heading, not the setting of the argument.
Every setting in the paper places AI systems among humans, institutions and infrastructure. Even §5's decisive pathway is one ASI acting on human subsystems, not agents interacting with agents.

The paper measures, evaluates and documents nothing. Monitoring appears only as something that must be built: 'we can develop more targeted monitoring mechanisms' (§7, Reply 2) and 'we need better methods' (§9, future work).

§8.1 proposes a tiered governance framework, but it names no specific institution, market or protocol to change. The proposal is governance direction, which §Steering already covers; tagging both double-counts one section.

§4 is a narrative thought experiment, not an agent-based model. System dynamics simulation appears only as future work: 'future efforts should aim to further validate and refine the accumulative hypothesis through system dynamic simulations'.
One clause in §2.3's list of social risk categories and two sentences in §4 ('top 0.1% now controlling over 70% of global wealth'). Never the harm under analysis.
One sentence in §4: 'The concentration of AI capabilities among a handful of tech conglomerates has exacerbated wealth inequality'. No heading, no analysis of who controls AI.

The blind spots the paper names are gaps in risk-governance coverage, not information asymmetry about what agents are doing. The paper analyses no hidden coordination, opaque collusion, or principal-agent opacity. The claim is counted once, under Outdated Models.

The paper's targets are models of AI risk, not models that were valid on a pre-AI human or algorithmic system: the decisive AI x-risk hypothesis, AI risk taxonomies, the NIST AI RMF and the EU AI Act categories. Human-judgment validation assumed a human rater can separate synthetic from human output; §5 states raters cannot, while computational comparison of the same text reveals substantial syntactical differences, so the test returns a pass where the objective measure returns a fail. no_value.system_type: The unit of study is one LLM at a time: an actor model's own elicited utility ranking and its own output quality. The judge panel and rubric coder are measurement apparatus, not a system of interacting agents under study. No named system_type clears the threshold, and the general purpose fallback requires a system of two or more AI agents.
no_value.public_observability: No passage establishes what an outsider, auditor or user sees. The paper describes a closed offline experiment run over an API; deployment, disclosure and third-party access are never discussed.

below_threshold.why: Old tag. The paper does manipulate prompts with incentives, effort instructions and role instructions (§4.3-§4.5), but only as control conditions that prove the pipeline can detect quality shifts. No governance, regulation or control of a deployed system is proposed. The paper is an empirical study with no policy section.

Old tag. Unequal valuation across nationalities, religions and species appears as prior work's finding in the abstract's motivation clause, and the same categories are reused as outcome domains for utility elicitation (§3.1). Unequal distribution of benefit or harm is never the object of study, has no heading, and is not the argument.

Considered. Three model roles exist in the pipeline (actor, judge panel, rubric coder), but they do not form a system the paper studies; they are the instrument. The claim is about a single model's preference-to-behavior link.

Considered. §5 proposes the paradigm for reuse: 'we suggest that it may usefully be applied to other investigations of motivated LLM behavior'. It is an evaluation method, not a new agent system, protocol or architecture, so Monitoring already covers it.

Considered. Emergent misaligned goals are the hypothesis the paper tests and argues against, but the value means goals arising at the group level that no individual agent holds. Here goals are attributed to single models, and there is no group.

Considered. The paper shows a stated-preference measurement fails to predict behaviour, which is about the validity of an inference, not about a principal being unable to see agent actions. No hidden coordination, collusion or information asymmetry is studied.

note: Kept Outdated Models on the strength of the title and abstract: the paper's central argument is that a standard measurement paradigm mis-describes the systems it is used on. Operator observability stops short of fully observable because Appendix B states the main experiments run with reasoning mode off, and no reasoning trace is ever inspected; the reasoning-enabled essay retest in §4.7 reports only outcomes.

outdated_models_recode.model: Pairwise utility elicitation (Thurstonian fit over forced choices), the revealed-preference instrument imported from human decision theory and used by Ross et al. 2024 and Mazeika et al. 2025 to read off LLM values
outdated_models_recode.assumption: that a coherent preference ordering revealed in choice is a motivating desire, so it predicts behaviour outside the choice paradigm
outdated_models_recode.quote: utility-elicitation methods for identifying preferences are not finding “desires” that motivate LLM behavior in the way that equivalent preferences in biological creatures might
outdated_models_recode.where: § 5 Discussion (restated in the abstract and the title)
outdated_models_recode.why: The paper names the standard utility-elicitation protocol, treats the preference-to-motivation inference as sound for humans and other biological creatures ("goals and desires, as we would call them in humans"), and states the assumption LLMs break: "pairwise utility elicitation establishes an evaluative ranking over outcomes; it does not establish that the preferred outcome motivates output generation." Seven actor models over four task families show high-utility consequences do not beat low-utility or no consequence on blind-judged quality, while effort, role and harm cues do move quality, so the instrument's safety reading is wrong rather than merely noisy. This is the title, the abstract's conclusion and the whole experiment, not an aside.

outdated_models_recode.quote: there exists a gap in zero-knowledge inferences over LLMs. The intricate structures and enormous sizes of LLMs present challenges not addressed by previous studies focused on CNNs, necessitating novel theoretical and experimental developments.

outdated_models_recode.why: Test 3 fails: the paper names prior zero-knowledge proof protocols for CNNs and MLPs as the thing LLMs defeat, but it identifies a coverage gap and an overhead problem, not an assumption falsified by AI. Test 4 fails with it: zkCNN and its peers stay sound on CNNs, they are simply too slow and too narrow for 13B-parameter transformers, so nothing starts giving wrong answers. The closest passages are § 9 above and the § 1 remark that Softmax sits after the output layer in MLPs and CNNs and so was 'not considered in prior works on zero-knowledge verifiable deep learning' - both are the paper's own novelty pitch for zkAttn and tlookup. The § 1 legal framing (NYT lawsuit, October 2023 executive order) is regulatory motivation by date, with no violated assumption named.
